citations.quote:
Fix an integer $m\ge1$. The **doubled line quiver** $\Gamma_m$ is the finite
quiver of [[def-path-ring-of-a-finite-quiver-over-the-integers]] with vertices
$0,1,\dots,m$ and, for every $0\le i\le m-1$, exactly two arrows between the
consecutive vertices $i$ and $i+1$, one in each direction. Its directed paths of
length $l$ are therefore the tuples
$$(i_1|i_2|\cdots|i_{l+1}),\qquad i_j\in\{0,1,\dots,m\},\quad |i_{j+1}-i_j|=1,$$
and the product of the path ring $\mathbb Z\Gamma_m$ is the left-to-right
concatenation of [[def-path-ring-of-a-finite-quiver-over-the-integers]].

**The algebra.** For $m\ge1$, let $I_m\trianglelefteq\mathbb Z\Gamma_m$ be the
two-sided ideal generated by the elements
$$(i-1|i|i+1),\qquad (i+1|i|i-1),\qquad (i|i+1|i)-(i|i-1|i),\qquad (0|1|0),$$
where the first three families are over all $0<i<m$; when $m=1$ the middle
family is empty and only $(0|1|0)$ is imposed. The **Khovanov–Seidel type A
algebra** is the quotient ring
$$A_m:=\mathbb Z\Gamma_m\big/I_m$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]), whose elements are written as cosets of paths.

**Internal degree.** The **internal degree** of a path is the integer
$$\deg(v_0|v_1|\cdots|v_l):=\#\{\,j:0\le j<l,\ v_{j+1}=v_j-1\,\},$$
the number of steps in which the path moves **down**; so a vertex and an
ascending arrow $(i|i+1)$ have degree $0$, while a descending arrow
$(i+1|i)$ has degree $1$. This number is additive under concatenation,
$\deg(pq)=\deg(p)+\deg(q)$.

**Grading.** Write $(\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_d$ for the free abelian group spanned by
the paths of degree $d$, so that $\mathbb Z\Gamma_m=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}(\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_d$
and $(\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_a(\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_b\subseteq(\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_{a+b}$
for all $a,b$. The quotient $A_m$ is graded,
$$A_m=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}(A_m)_d,\qquad (A_m)_d:=\bigl((\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_d+I_m\bigr)/I_m,$$
with $(A_m)_a(A_m)_b\subseteq(A_m)_{a+b}$ and $1_{A_m}\in(A_m)_0$, as proved
below. Elements of $(A_m)_d$ are called homogeneous of degree $d$, and
homogeneous elements of the two lowest degrees are written
$$e_i:=(i),\qquad u_i:=(i|i+1),\qquad d_i:=(i+1|i)\qquad(0\le i\le m-1),$$
so that $\deg e_i=0=\deg u_i$ and $\deg d_i=1$. In keeping with the tuple
notation of the path ring, the left entry of $(i+1|i)$ is its source, so
$(i+1|i)$ is the arrow from $i+1$ to $i$; likewise $(i-1|i|i+1)$ is the
two-step path $i-1\to i\to i+1$ and $(i|i-1|i)$ is the return $i\to i-1\to i$.

A **finite quiver** is a quadruple $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$ in which $Q_0$ and $Q_1$
are finite sets, whose elements are called **vertices** and **arrows**, together
with maps $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$ assigning to an arrow $a$ its **source** $s(a)$ and
its **target** $t(a)$; one draws $a:s(a)\to t(a)$. Both sets are finite and no
further structure is assumed: $Q$ may have several arrows with the same source
and target, and an arrow may be a loop, although the quivers used below have
neither property.

A **directed path** in $Q$ of length $l\ge0$ consists of vertices
$v_0,\ldots,v_l$ and specified arrows $a_j:v_{j-1}\to v_j$ for $1\le j\le l$.
Write it as $p=(v_0\xrightarrow{a_1}v_1\xrightarrow{a_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{a_l}v_l)$.
The arrows are part of the data: distinct parallel arrows give distinct paths.
A path of length zero is a single vertex $(v)$, called a **vertex idempotent**.
Write $|p|:=l$, $s(p):=v_0$ and $t(p):=v_l$ for its **length**, **source** and
**target**. When the arrows are determined by their endpoints, as in the doubled
lines used below, abbreviate this by $(v_0|\cdots|v_l)$; in formulas for a
general quiver this abbreviation retains the specified arrows as implicit data.
Paths $p$ and $q$ are **composable** if $t(p)=s(q)$. Their **concatenation**
$pq$ traverses the arrow sequence of $p$ first and then that of $q$, retaining
all arrow labels; in the abbreviated notation it is
$$(v_0|\cdots|v_l)(v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'})=(v_0|\cdots|v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'}).$$

The **integral path ring** $\mathbb ZQ$ is the free abelian group on the set of
all directed paths of $Q$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]),
with multiplication defined on basis paths by
$$(v_0|\cdots|v_l)(w_0|\cdots|w_{l'}):= \begin{cases}(v_0|\cdots|v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'}),&v_l=w_0,\\ 0,&v_l\ne w_0,\end{cases}$$
and extended by $\mathbb Z$-bilinearity. Its unit is the finite sum
$$1_{\mathbb ZQ}=\sum_{v\in Q_0}(v)$$
of the vertex idempotents, which is a finite sum because $Q_0$ is finite.

**Endpoint conventions.** For a path $p$ and vertices $u,v$ one has
$$(u)\,p=\begin{cases}p,&s(p)=u,\\ 0,&s(p)\ne u,\end{cases} \qquad p\,(v)=\begin{cases}p,&t(p)=v,\\ 0,&t(p)\ne v.\end{cases}$$
Consequently the vertex idempotents are mutually orthogonal,
$(u)(v)=\delta_{uv}(v)$, and they decompose the ring as
$$\mathbb ZQ=\bigoplus_{u,v\in Q_0}(u)\,\mathbb ZQ\,(v),$$
the sum of the free abelian groups spanned by the paths with source $u$ and
target $v$. In the quotient rings used below, the analogous statements read:
the right ideal generated by the image of $(u)$ is spanned by the classes of paths with source
$u$, and the left ideal generated by the image of $(v)$ is spanned by the classes of paths with target
$v$, so that $A\,e_i$ consists of the paths **ending** at $i$ and $e_iA$ of the
paths **beginning** at $i$ whenever $A$ is a quotient of $\mathbb ZQ$ and
$e_i$ is the image of $(i)$.

**Empty quiver.** For $Q_0=Q_1=\varnothing$ the set of paths is empty, so
$\mathbb ZQ$ is the zero abelian group, the displayed sum for $1$ is empty and
$1=0$; this is the zero ring, and every statement below is trivial there. All
quivers occurring on this page are the doubled lines $\Gamma_m$ with $m\ge1$,
which have $m+1\ge2$ vertices.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]]. As a graded abelian group $A_m$
is free of rank $4m+1$, with basis the images of the $4m+1$ paths
$$(0),\dots,(m);\qquad (0|1),\dots,(m-1|m);\qquad (1|0),\dots,(m|m-1);\qquad (1|0|1),\dots,(m|m-1|m),$$
that is: the $m+1$ vertices, the $2m$ arrows, and one degree-one length-two
**return** at each vertex $i=1,\dots,m$. Every path of length at least three has
class $0$ in $A_m$, the monotone length-two path $(i-1|i|i+1)$ and its reverse
$(i+1|i|i-1)$ have class $0$ for $0<i<m$, the return $(0|1|0)$ has class $0$,
and at an interior vertex $0<i<m$ the two returns $(i|i+1|i)$ and $(i|i-1|i)$
have the same class. In particular $A_m$ is a finitely generated free abelian
group, so its underlying $\mathbb Z$-module is free of finite rank $4m+1$.

Fix $m\ge1$ and let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]], graded by internal degree, with
the vertex idempotents $e_i:=(i)$ and the generators $u_i:=(i|i+1)$,
$d_i:=(i+1|i)$.

**The finite module category.** $A_m\text{-mod}$ is the category whose objects
are the **finitely generated graded left $A_m$-modules** and whose morphisms are
the **degree-zero $A_m$-linear maps** $f:M\to N$, that is
$f(M_d)\subseteq N_d$ for every $d$, with composition of maps. Throughout this
page every left module, right module and bimodule over $A_m$ is graded and every
homomorphism is degree-zero unless stated otherwise. Finite generation is in the
sense of [[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]], and graded
modules, degree-zero maps and internal shifts are those of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]].

**Internal shift.** For $r\in\mathbb Z$ and a graded left $A_m$-module $M$ the
**internal shift** $M\{r\}$ is the graded module with
$$(M\{r\})_d=M_{d-r}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
carrying the same left $A_m$-action as $M$. The shift $\{1\}$ moves the grading
upwards by one: an element of $M_d$ is an element of $(M\{1\})_{d+1}$.

**Vertex projectives.** Put
$$P_i:=A_me_i,\qquad {}_iP:=e_iA_m\qquad(0\le i\le m),$$
equipped with the grading in which a homogeneous element of $A_m$ of degree $d$
lies in degree $d$. Because paths are written left to right and the product is
concatenation, $P_i$ consists of the classes of the paths **ending** at $i$ and
${}_iP$ of the classes of the paths **beginning** at $i$. The algebra splits as
$$A_m=\bigoplus_{i=0}^mP_i=\bigoplus_{i=0}^m{}_iP$$
as a left, respectively right, module over itself; the decomposition into vertex
projectives is displayed as proved below.

**Claims proved below.** $A_m\text{-mod}$ is an abelian category; the internal
shift $\{r\}$ is an automorphism of $A_m\text{-mod}$; each $P_i$ is a finite
graded projective left $A_m$-module and each ${}_iP$ a finite graded projective
right $A_m$-module, generated by $e_i$.

**Notation.** The source writes $P_i=A_m(i)$ for the summand $A_me_i$, and
$\{r\}$ for the internal shift; the parentheses in $A_m(i)$ are part of that
summand notation and never denote a shift. On this page only the braces $\{r\}$
denote the internal shift, and only the brackets $[r]$ of
[[def-bounded-projective-homotopy-category-for-a-m]] denote the homological
shift, which is not defined yet.

Fix $m\ge1$, let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]] with vertex idempotents
$e_j=(j)$ and internal degree, and let $A_m\text{-mod}$ be the category of
[[def-graded-khovanov-seidel-module-category-and-projectives]].

**The vertex modules.** For $0\le i\le m$ let $S_i$ be the graded left
$A_m$-module whose underlying graded abelian group is
$$(S_i)_0=\mathbb Z,\qquad (S_i)_d=0\quad(d\ne0),$$
and on which a path $p$ of $\mathbb Z\Gamma_m$ acts by
$$e_i\cdot1=1,\qquad e_j\cdot1=0\ (j\ne i),\qquad p\cdot1=0\text{ for every positive-length path }p.$$
Equivalently, $e_i$ acts as the identity, every other vertex idempotent acts as
zero, and every path of positive length acts as zero. The claims that this
assignment is well defined on the quotient $A_m$, that it makes $S_i$ a
finitely generated graded left $A_m$-module and that it is not the zero module
are proved below, so the notation denotes.

**Prime quotients.** For a prime $p$, $pS_i$ is the $A_m$-submodule generated
by $p\cdot1$ and $S_i/pS_i$ is the quotient module; it is the corresponding
$\mathbb Z/p$ **vertex module**, that is the graded left $A_m$-module
$(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)$ in internal degree $0$, with the induced action in
which $e_i$ acts as the identity and every other vertex idempotent and every
positive-length path acts as zero. The sequence
$$0\to S_i\xrightarrow{p}S_i\to S_i/pS_i\to0$$
is degreewise exact for every prime $p$; exactness at both non-end terms is
proved below, so the notation denotes.

**Shifts.** The internal shifts of $S_i$ are inherited from $A_m\text{-mod}$:
$S_i\{r\}$ is the internal shift of the definition of
[[def-graded-khovanov-seidel-module-category-and-projectives]], so that
$(S_i\{r\})_{r}=\mathbb Z$ and all other graded pieces vanish and the same
action rule applies. The vertex module $S_i$ is the quotient of the vertex
projective $P_i=A_me_i$ by its positive-length-path submodule; the
identifications with the quotients $P_i/A_m\{u_{i-1},d_i,r_i\}$ (omitting $u_{-1}$, $d_m$ and $r_0$ at the endpoints, and writing $r_i=(i|i-1|i)$ for $1\le i\le m$) and with the
$\mathbb Z/p$ reductions are proved on the pages that use them.

Let $A$ be an object of an abelian category. A **projective resolution of $A$** is an augmented chain complex $$\cdots \to P_2\to P_1\to P_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A\to0$$ such that every $P_n$ is projective and the augmented complex is exact at every displayed term.

Thus a projective resolution is an exact way of recovering $A$ from projective objects arranged in homological degrees.

In an abelian category, a **homological double complex** consists of objects
$C_{p,q}$ for all $(p,q)\in\mathbb Z^2$ and morphisms
$$h_{p,q}:C_{p,q}\longrightarrow C_{p-1,q},\qquad v_{p,q}:C_{p,q}\longrightarrow C_{p,q-1}.$$
For every pair of integers they satisfy
$$h_{p-1,q}h_{p,q}=0,\qquad v_{p,q-1}v_{p,q}=0,\qquad h_{p,q-1}v_{p,q}+v_{p-1,q}h_{p,q}=0.$$
The third equality is in $\operatorname{Hom}(C_{p,q},C_{p-1,q-1})$.
The first two equalities say that every row and every column is a
[[def-chain-complex-in-an-abelian-category|chain complex]]. They are separate
axioms; anticommutation alone does not imply them.

A morphism $f:C\to D$ consists of maps $f_{p,q}:C_{p,q}\to D_{p,q}$ with
$$f_{p-1,q}h^C_{p,q}=h^D_{p,q}f_{p,q},\qquad f_{p,q-1}v^C_{p,q}=v^D_{p,q}f_{p,q}.$$
Identities and composition are componentwise. The complex is **first
quadrant** if $C_{p,q}=0$ whenever $p<0$ or $q<0$.

Zero objects and complexes supported at one bidegree are allowed. Arrows
meeting a zero object are zero, including the outgoing arrows on the axes of
a first-quadrant complex. This definition requires no infinite products,
coproducts, or choices of representatives.

Let $C$ be a [[def-homological-double-complex|homological double complex]] in
an abelian category. Suppose that for every integer $n$ the diagonal
[[def-products-and-coproducts|coproduct]] below exists, and write its injections
as $\iota^n_{p,q}$:
$$T_n=\operatorname{Tot}^{\oplus}_n(C)=\coprod_{p+q=n}C_{p,q}.$$
Define $d_n:T_n\to T_{n-1}$ to be the unique arrow with
$$d_n\iota^n_{p,q}=\iota^{n-1}_{p-1,q}h_{p,q}+\iota^{n-1}_{p,q-1}v_{p,q}\quad(p+q=n).$$
Each right-hand side is the sum of two morphisms with the same source and
target. The coproduct universal property supplies a unique $d_n$ from this
family; no infinite sum in a morphism group is required.

The resulting **direct-sum total complex** has differential of degree $-1$.
Its chain condition is established in
[[lem-the-total-differential-squares-to-zero]]. A diagonal with only zero
objects has zero coproduct: every family of maps from its objects is the
unique zero family. A diagonal with exactly one nonzero object has that
object as coproduct. For general infinite diagonals existence is a hypothesis,
not an implication of being an abelian category. No choices of elements or
representatives enter this construction.

For the direct-sum totalisation of an anticommuting homological double
complex, $d_{n-1}d_n=0$ for every integer $n$.

Let $C$ be a first-quadrant homological double complex in an abelian category.
If $H^v_q(C_{p,*})=0$ for every $p$ and every $q>0$, put
$B_p=H^v_0(C_{p,*})$ with differential induced by $h$. The natural projection
$\rho:\operatorname{Tot}(C)\to B$, given on $C_{n,0}$ by the quotient map
and zero on other summands in degree $n$, is a quasi-isomorphism.

If instead $H^h_p(C_{*,q})=0$ for $p>0$, the analogous projection to
$(H^h_0(C_{*,q}),v)$ is a quasi-isomorphism. In particular completely acyclic
columns or completely acyclic rows imply an acyclic total complex.

Let $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ be a chain map in an additive category. The
**mapping cone** of $f$ is the chain complex $\operatorname{Cone}(f)_\bullet$
whose degree-$n$ term is
$$\operatorname{Cone}(f)_n:=D_n\oplus C[1]_n=D_n\oplus C_{n-1},$$
and whose differential is
$$d_n^{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}(y,x):=(d_n^D(y)+f_{n-1}(x),-d_{n-1}^C(x)).$$

Thus $\operatorname{Cone}(f)$ is the direct sum of $D$ and the shift $C[1]$ as
a graded object, with the off-diagonal term given by $f$.

For every chain map $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ in an abelian category, the
sequence
$$0\to D_\bullet\xrightarrow{j}\operatorname{Cone}(f)_\bullet\xrightarrow{q}C[1]_\bullet\to0$$
from [[def-canonical-inclusion-and-projection-for-a-mapping-cone]] is a short
exact sequence of complexes, and in each degree it is split short exact in the
ambient abelian category.

Let
$$0\to A_\bullet\to B_\bullet\to C_\bullet\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of complexes in an abelian category. Then there is an
exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A)\to H_n(B)\to H_n(C)\xrightarrow{\partial_n}H_{n-1}(A)\to H_{n-1}(B)\to H_{n-1}(C)\to\cdots.$$

An object $P$ of an abelian category is **projective** when for every epimorphism
$q:E\twoheadrightarrow M$ and every morphism $f:P\to M$, there exists a
morphism $\widetilde f:P\to E$ with

$$q\widetilde f=f.$$

The lift $\widetilde f$ need not be unique.

A chain map $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ is a **quasi-isomorphism** if for every
$n\in\mathbb Z$ the induced map
$$H_n(f):H_n(C)\to H_n(D)$$
is an isomorphism.

derivations.claim: *Basis and products in the vertex projectives.* By [L3] the $4m+1$ displayed classes form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $A_m$, and each basis path has a source and a target, so by [F2] the module $P_j=A_me_j$ has the $\mathbb Z$-basis consisting of $e_j$ together with the basis paths ending at $j$, namely $e_j$; $u_{j-1}=(j-1|j)$; $d_j=(j+1|j)$; $r_j$, a symbol being omitted when the arrow has no source or target in $\{0,\dots,m\}$. Thus $P_j$ has basis $\{e_j,u_{j-1},d_j,r_j\}$ for $0<j<m$, basis $\{e_0,d_0\}$ for $j=0$ (since $(0|1|0)$ has class $0$ and $u_{-1}$ does not exist) and basis $\{e_m,u_{m-1},r_m\}$ for $j=m$ (since $d_m$ does not exist). For the multiplication we use [F1], [F2] and [L3]: $xe_j=x$ for $x\in P_j$, while $e_je_j=e_j$; $u_{j-1}u_j$ is a monotone length-two path, hence $0$ by [F1], while $r_ju_j$ and $r_jd_{j-1}$ are classes of paths of length three, hence $0$; and $d_ju_j=(j+1|j|j+1)$ is the return at $j+1$, which is exactly the basis return $r_{j+1}=(j+1|j|j+1)$.

*The staircase is a first-quadrant double complex in $A_m\text{-mod}$.* The entries $C_{p,q}=P_{j(p,q)}\{p\}$ are graded left $A_m$-modules, vanish for $p<0$ or $q<0$, and are nonzero exactly on $0\le p\le m-i$, $0\le q\le i+p$; the staircase condition $q\le i+p$ means $j(p,q)\ge0$, and $p\le m-i$ means $j(p,q)=i+p-q\le i+p\le m$, so the projective indices are in range. When both source and target entries are nonzero, right multiplication by $\alpha=(j|j-1)$ carries $P_j$ into $P_j\alpha\subseteq P_{j-1}$, and by [L4] it is a degree-zero module map $P_j\{p\}\to P_{j-1}\{p-1\}$ because $\deg\alpha=1$ exactly compensates the drop of the shift; right multiplication by $\beta=(j|j+1)$ carries $P_j$ into $P_{j+1}$ and is degree-zero as a map $P_j\{p\}\to P_{j+1}\{p\}$ because $\deg\beta=0$. Hence $h_{p,q}:C_{p,q}\to C_{p-1,q}$ and $v_{p,q}:C_{p,q}\to C_{p,q-1}$ are degree-zero module maps, the sign $(-1)^p$ being a unit of the ground ring. On $C_{p,q}$, $h^2$ is right multiplication by the monotone length-two path $(j|j-1|j-2)$, hence is $0$ by [F1] (and $h^2=0$ at the boundary, where one of the two symbols does not exist); similarly $v^2$ is right multiplication by the monotone length-two path $(j|j+1|j+2)=0$ by [F1], and $hv+vh$ is right multiplication by $(-1)^{p-1}(j|j-1|j)+(-1)^p(j|j+1|j)=(-1)^{p-1}\bigl[(j|j-1|j)-(j|j+1|j)\bigr]=0$ by the relation of [F1]. For the mixed relation at the staircase boundary, if $p=0$ or $q=0$ both composites have zero target. If $p,q>0$ and $j=0$, the horizontal-first composite vanishes and the vertical-first composite multiplies by $(0|1|0)=0$. In all other nonzero mixed squares $0<j<m$, so the displayed return relation applies. Maps with zero source or target are zero by convention; the same convention handles the boundary cases of $h^2$ and $v^2$. Thus $(C,h,v)$ satisfies [L7].

*The columns are exact above their top entry.* Fix $0\le j\le m-1$ and $x=\alpha e_j+\beta u_{j-1}+\gamma d_j+\delta r_j\in P_j$. By the product rules of step 1.1, $xu_j=\alpha u_j+\beta u_{j-1}u_j+\gamma d_ju_j+\delta r_ju_j=\alpha u_j+\gamma r_{j+1}$, so by basis independence $xu_j=0$ if and only if $\alpha=\gamma=0$, that is, if and only if $x\in\mathbb Zu_{j-1}\oplus\mathbb Zr_j$. On the other hand right multiplication by $u_{j-1}$ on $P_{j-1}$ has image $\{x'u_{j-1}\}$ spanned by $e_{j-1}u_{j-1}=u_{j-1}$ and $d_{j-1}u_{j-1}=r_j$, the other two basis products being $0$ by step 1.1; so the image is $\mathbb Zu_{j-1}\oplus\mathbb Zr_j$ and $\ker(x\mapsto xu_j)=\operatorname{im}(x'\mapsto x'u_{j-1})$. For $j=0$ the same computation gives $xu_0=\alpha u_0+\gamma r_1$ (using $r_0=0$ by [L3]); the two images are independent basis classes, so the kernel is $0=\operatorname{im}(x'\mapsto x'u_{-1})$, with $P_{-1}=0$. In the column $C_{p,*}$ the maps $v$ multiply by $u_{i+p-q}$ and the statement just proved identifies, for every $q\ge1$, the kernel of $v:C_{p,q}\to C_{p,q-1}$ with the image of $v:C_{p,q+1}\to C_{p,q}$, since $C_{p,q+1}=P_{j-1}\{p\}$ and $C_{p,q-1}=P_{j+1}\{p\}$; hence $H^v_q(C_{p,*})=0$ for every $p$ and every $q>0$.

*The bottom row of the assembled complex.* By step 2.2 and [L7], $B_p:=H^v_0(C_{p,*})=C_{p,0}/\operatorname{im}(v:C_{p,1}\to C_{p,0})$ for $0\le p\le m-i$, where $C_{p,0}=P_{i+p}\{p\}$ and the image is $P_{i+p-1}u_{i+p-1}=\mathbb Zu_{i+p-1}\oplus\mathbb Zr_{i+p}$ for $i+p\ge1$ and $0$ for $i=p=0$; the differential $h$ descends to $B$ by the anticommutation proved in step 2.1. So $B_p$ is the quotient of $P_{i+p}$ by the $\mathbb Z$-span of $u_{i+p-1}$ and $r_{i+p}$, with $\mathbb Z$-basis the classes $[e_{i+p}]$ and $[d_{i+p}]$ when $i+p<m$, and basis $[e_m]$ when $i+p=m$. On these classes $h:B_p\to B_{p-1}$ is induced by right multiplication by $d_{i+p-1}$, and by step 1.1 it sends $[e_{i+p}]\mapsto[d_{i+p-1}]$ and $[d_{i+p}]\mapsto[d_{i+p}d_{i+p-1}]=0$.

*The homology of the bottom row is $S_i$.* Since $h_1:B_1\to B_0$ has image $\mathbb Z[d_i]$ (and is $0$ when $m=i$), $H_0(B)=B_0/\mathbb Z[d_i]=\mathbb Z[e_i]$; the quotient $C_{0,0}=P_i$ modulo the span of $u_{i-1},d_i,r_i$ is the quotient of $P_i$ by $A_mu_{i-1}+A_md_i$, which by step 1.1 equals the submodule generated by all positive-length paths ending at $i$, so $H_0(B)$ is $\mathbb Z$ in degree $0$ with $e_i$ acting as the identity and every other vertex idempotent and every positive-length path acting as zero: by [L5] this is exactly $S_i$. For $1\le p<m-i$, step 3.1 gives $\ker h_p=\mathbb Z[d_{i+p}]=\operatorname{im}h_{p+1}$, while at $p=m-i\ge1$ the group $B_p=\mathbb Z[e_m]$ maps injectively to $B_{p-1}$, so its kernel is $0=\operatorname{im}h_{p+1}$; when $i=m$ there are no positive-degree $B_p$ at all. Hence $H_p(B)=\ker h_p/\operatorname{im}h_{p+1}=0$ for every $p\ge1$.

*Totalisation is a finite graded projective resolution of $S_i$.* Step 2.2 verifies the hypothesis of [L8], so the projection $\operatorname{Tot}(C)\to B$ is a quasi-isomorphism; by step 4.1 and [L10] therefore $H_0(\operatorname{Tot})\cong S_i$ and $H_n(\operatorname{Tot})=0$ for $n\ne0$. Each $\operatorname{Tot}_n$ is the finite direct sum of the $C_{p,q}=P_{j(p,q)}\{p\}$ with $p+q=n$, a finite direct sum of internal shifts of vertex projectives; each $P_j$ is finite graded projective by [L4], its shift is finite graded projective because $\{p\}$ is an automorphism of $A_m\text{-mod}$ by [L4], and a finite direct sum of projective objects is projective by the lifting property applied componentwise with the universal property of the coproduct, so every term of $\operatorname{Tot}$ is finite graded projective. Only the finitely many degrees $0\le n\le m+(m-i)$ can be nonzero, and the differential satisfies $d^2=0$ by [L7]. The augmentation $\varepsilon:\operatorname{Tot}_0=C_{0,0}=P_i\to S_i$ is the quotient map of step 4.1; since the projection of [L8], followed by the augmentation $B_0\to S_i$, restricts to this quotient on $C_{0,0}$, the augmented complex is exact at $P_i$ and at every other term, so by [L6] $\operatorname{Tot}$ is a finite graded projective resolution of $S_i$.

*The cone of multiplication by $p$ resolves $S_i/pS_i$.* Multiplication by the integer $p$ is an $A_m$-linear endomorphism of each $P_j$ preserving degrees, so it defines a degree-zero chain map $\mu_p:\operatorname{Tot}_\bullet\to\operatorname{Tot}_\bullet$. By [L9] the cone has $\operatorname{Cone}(\mu_p)_n=\operatorname{Tot}_n\oplus\operatorname{Tot}_{n-1}$, a finite direct sum of finite graded projectives, and there is a degreewise split short exact sequence of complexes $0\to\operatorname{Tot}\to\operatorname{Cone}(\mu_p)\to\operatorname{Tot}[1]\to0$ whose long exact homology sequence reads $H_n(\operatorname{Tot})\xrightarrow{\mu_p}H_n(\operatorname{Tot})\to H_n(\operatorname{Cone}(\mu_p))\to H_{n-1}(\operatorname{Tot})\xrightarrow{\mu_p}H_{n-1}(\operatorname{Tot})$. By step 5.1 the only nonzero homology of $\operatorname{Tot}$ is $H_0=S_i$; hence $H_0(\operatorname{Cone}(\mu_p))=\operatorname{coker}(p:S_i\to S_i)=S_i/pS_i$, $H_1(\operatorname{Cone}(\mu_p))=\ker(p:S_i\to S_i)=0$ because $S_i=\mathbb Z$ is torsion free and $p\ne0$, and $H_n(\operatorname{Cone}(\mu_p))=0$ for $n\ge2$ and for $n\le-1$. So the cone is a finite complex of finite graded projectives whose only homology is $S_i/pS_i$ in degree $0$, that is, a finite graded projective resolution of $S_i/pS_i$ in the sense of [L6].

*Conclusion.* The double complex $(C,h,v)$ of step 2.1 is first quadrant, its columns are exact above the top entry by step 2.2, and its total complex is the finite graded projective resolution of $S_i$ described in claim 1 (steps 4.1 and 5.1); the mapping cone of multiplication by $p$ on it is the finite graded projective resolution of $S_i/pS_i$ described in claim 2 (step 6.1). **The finite module category.** $A_m\text{-mod}$ is the category whose objects
are the **finitely generated graded left $A_m$-modules** and whose morphisms are
the **degree-zero $A_m$-linear maps** $f:M\to N$, that is
$f(M_d)\subseteq N_d$ for every $d$, with composition of maps. Throughout this
page every left module, right module and bimodule over $A_m$ is graded and every
homomorphism is degree-zero unless stated otherwise. Finite generation is in the
sense of [[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]], and graded
modules, degree-zero maps and internal shifts are those of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]].

Let $m\ge1$ and let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]]. As a graded abelian group $A_m$
is free of rank $4m+1$, with basis the images of the $4m+1$ paths
$$(0),\dots,(m);\qquad (0|1),\dots,(m-1|m);\qquad (1|0),\dots,(m|m-1);\qquad (1|0|1),\dots,(m|m-1|m),$$
that is: the $m+1$ vertices, the $2m$ arrows, and one degree-one length-two
**return** at each vertex $i=1,\dots,m$. Every path of length at least three has
class $0$ in $A_m$, the monotone length-two path $(i-1|i|i+1)$ and its reverse
$(i+1|i|i-1)$ have class $0$ for $0<i<m$, the return $(0|1|0)$ has class $0$,
and at an interior vertex $0<i<m$ the two returns $(i|i+1|i)$ and $(i|i-1|i)$
have the same class. In particular $A_m$ is a finitely generated free abelian
group, so its underlying $\mathbb Z$-module is free of finite rank $4m+1$.

Fix an integer $m\ge1$. The **doubled line quiver** $\Gamma_m$ is the finite
quiver of [[def-path-ring-of-a-finite-quiver-over-the-integers]] with vertices
$0,1,\dots,m$ and, for every $0\le i\le m-1$, exactly two arrows between the
consecutive vertices $i$ and $i+1$, one in each direction. Its directed paths of
length $l$ are therefore the tuples
$$(i_1|i_2|\cdots|i_{l+1}),\qquad i_j\in\{0,1,\dots,m\},\quad |i_{j+1}-i_j|=1,$$
and the product of the path ring $\mathbb Z\Gamma_m$ is the left-to-right
concatenation of [[def-path-ring-of-a-finite-quiver-over-the-integers]].

**The algebra.** For $m\ge1$, let $I_m\trianglelefteq\mathbb Z\Gamma_m$ be the
two-sided ideal generated by the elements
$$(i-1|i|i+1),\qquad (i+1|i|i-1),\qquad (i|i+1|i)-(i|i-1|i),\qquad (0|1|0),$$
where the first three families are over all $0<i<m$; when $m=1$ the middle
family is empty and only $(0|1|0)$ is imposed. The **Khovanov–Seidel type A
algebra** is the quotient ring
$$A_m:=\mathbb Z\Gamma_m\big/I_m$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]), whose elements are written as cosets of paths.

**Internal degree.** The **internal degree** of a path is the integer
$$\deg(v_0|v_1|\cdots|v_l):=\#\{\,j:0\le j<l,\ v_{j+1}=v_j-1\,\},$$
the number of steps in which the path moves **down**; so a vertex and an
ascending arrow $(i|i+1)$ have degree $0$, while a descending arrow
$(i+1|i)$ has degree $1$. This number is additive under concatenation,
$\deg(pq)=\deg(p)+\deg(q)$.

**Grading.** Write $(\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_d$ for the free abelian group spanned by
the paths of degree $d$, so that $\mathbb Z\Gamma_m=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}(\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_d$
and $(\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_a(\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_b\subseteq(\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_{a+b}$
for all $a,b$. The quotient $A_m$ is graded,
$$A_m=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}(A_m)_d,\qquad (A_m)_d:=\bigl((\mathbb Z\Gamma_m)_d+I_m\bigr)/I_m,$$
with $(A_m)_a(A_m)_b\subseteq(A_m)_{a+b}$ and $1_{A_m}\in(A_m)_0$, as proved
below. Elements of $(A_m)_d$ are called homogeneous of degree $d$, and
homogeneous elements of the two lowest degrees are written
$$e_i:=(i),\qquad u_i:=(i|i+1),\qquad d_i:=(i+1|i)\qquad(0\le i\le m-1),$$
so that $\deg e_i=0=\deg u_i$ and $\deg d_i=1$. In keeping with the tuple
notation of the path ring, the left entry of $(i+1|i)$ is its source, so
$(i+1|i)$ is the arrow from $i+1$ to $i$; likewise $(i-1|i|i+1)$ is the
two-step path $i-1\to i\to i+1$ and $(i|i-1|i)$ is the return $i\to i-1\to i$.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]]. As a graded abelian group $A_m$
is free of rank $4m+1$, with basis the images of the $4m+1$ paths
$$(0),\dots,(m);\qquad (0|1),\dots,(m-1|m);\qquad (1|0),\dots,(m|m-1);\qquad (1|0|1),\dots,(m|m-1|m),$$
that is: the $m+1$ vertices, the $2m$ arrows, and one degree-one length-two
**return** at each vertex $i=1,\dots,m$. Every path of length at least three has
class $0$ in $A_m$, the monotone length-two path $(i-1|i|i+1)$ and its reverse
$(i+1|i|i-1)$ have class $0$ for $0<i<m$, the return $(0|1|0)$ has class $0$,
and at an interior vertex $0<i<m$ the two returns $(i|i+1|i)$ and $(i|i-1|i)$
have the same class. In particular $A_m$ is a finitely generated free abelian
group, so its underlying $\mathbb Z$-module is free of finite rank $4m+1$.

A **finite quiver** is a quadruple $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$ in which $Q_0$ and $Q_1$
are finite sets, whose elements are called **vertices** and **arrows**, together
with maps $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$ assigning to an arrow $a$ its **source** $s(a)$ and
its **target** $t(a)$; one draws $a:s(a)\to t(a)$. Both sets are finite and no
further structure is assumed: $Q$ may have several arrows with the same source
and target, and an arrow may be a loop, although the quivers used below have
neither property.

A **directed path** in $Q$ of length $l\ge0$ consists of vertices
$v_0,\ldots,v_l$ and specified arrows $a_j:v_{j-1}\to v_j$ for $1\le j\le l$.
Write it as $p=(v_0\xrightarrow{a_1}v_1\xrightarrow{a_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{a_l}v_l)$.
The arrows are part of the data: distinct parallel arrows give distinct paths.
A path of length zero is a single vertex $(v)$, called a **vertex idempotent**.
Write $|p|:=l$, $s(p):=v_0$ and $t(p):=v_l$ for its **length**, **source** and
**target**. When the arrows are determined by their endpoints, as in the doubled
lines used below, abbreviate this by $(v_0|\cdots|v_l)$; in formulas for a
general quiver this abbreviation retains the specified arrows as implicit data.
Paths $p$ and $q$ are **composable** if $t(p)=s(q)$. Their **concatenation**
$pq$ traverses the arrow sequence of $p$ first and then that of $q$, retaining
all arrow labels; in the abbreviated notation it is
$$(v_0|\cdots|v_l)(v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'})=(v_0|\cdots|v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'}).$$

The **integral path ring** $\mathbb ZQ$ is the free abelian group on the set of
all directed paths of $Q$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]),
with multiplication defined on basis paths by
$$(v_0|\cdots|v_l)(w_0|\cdots|w_{l'}):= \begin{cases}(v_0|\cdots|v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'}),&v_l=w_0,\\ 0,&v_l\ne w_0,\end{cases}$$
and extended by $\mathbb Z$-bilinearity. Its unit is the finite sum
$$1_{\mathbb ZQ}=\sum_{v\in Q_0}(v)$$
of the vertex idempotents, which is a finite sum because $Q_0$ is finite.

**Endpoint conventions.** For a path $p$ and vertices $u,v$ one has
$$(u)\,p=\begin{cases}p,&s(p)=u,\\ 0,&s(p)\ne u,\end{cases} \qquad p\,(v)=\begin{cases}p,&t(p)=v,\\ 0,&t(p)\ne v.\end{cases}$$
Consequently the vertex idempotents are mutually orthogonal,
$(u)(v)=\delta_{uv}(v)$, and they decompose the ring as
$$\mathbb ZQ=\bigoplus_{u,v\in Q_0}(u)\,\mathbb ZQ\,(v),$$
the sum of the free abelian groups spanned by the paths with source $u$ and
target $v$. In the quotient rings used below, the analogous statements read:
the right ideal generated by the image of $(u)$ is spanned by the classes of paths with source
$u$, and the left ideal generated by the image of $(v)$ is spanned by the classes of paths with target
$v$, so that $A\,e_i$ consists of the paths **ending** at $i$ and $e_iA$ of the
paths **beginning** at $i$ whenever $A$ is a quotient of $\mathbb ZQ$ and
$e_i$ is the image of $(i)$.

**Empty quiver.** For $Q_0=Q_1=\varnothing$ the set of paths is empty, so
$\mathbb ZQ$ is the zero abelian group, the displayed sum for $1$ is empty and
$1=0$; this is the zero ring, and every statement below is trivial there. All
quivers occurring on this page are the doubled lines $\Gamma_m$ with $m\ge1$,
which have $m+1\ge2$ vertices.

Fix $m\ge1$ and let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]], graded by internal degree, with
the vertex idempotents $e_i:=(i)$ and the generators $u_i:=(i|i+1)$,
$d_i:=(i+1|i)$.

**The finite module category.** $A_m\text{-mod}$ is the category whose objects
are the **finitely generated graded left $A_m$-modules** and whose morphisms are
the **degree-zero $A_m$-linear maps** $f:M\to N$, that is
$f(M_d)\subseteq N_d$ for every $d$, with composition of maps. Throughout this
page every left module, right module and bimodule over $A_m$ is graded and every
homomorphism is degree-zero unless stated otherwise. Finite generation is in the
sense of [[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]], and graded
modules, degree-zero maps and internal shifts are those of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]].

**Internal shift.** For $r\in\mathbb Z$ and a graded left $A_m$-module $M$ the
**internal shift** $M\{r\}$ is the graded module with
$$(M\{r\})_d=M_{d-r}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
carrying the same left $A_m$-action as $M$. The shift $\{1\}$ moves the grading
upwards by one: an element of $M_d$ is an element of $(M\{1\})_{d+1}$.

**Vertex projectives.** Put
$$P_i:=A_me_i,\qquad {}_iP:=e_iA_m\qquad(0\le i\le m),$$
equipped with the grading in which a homogeneous element of $A_m$ of degree $d$
lies in degree $d$. Because paths are written left to right and the product is
concatenation, $P_i$ consists of the classes of the paths **ending** at $i$ and
${}_iP$ of the classes of the paths **beginning** at $i$. The algebra splits as
$$A_m=\bigoplus_{i=0}^mP_i=\bigoplus_{i=0}^m{}_iP$$
as a left, respectively right, module over itself; the decomposition into vertex
projectives is displayed as proved below.

**Claims proved below.** $A_m\text{-mod}$ is an abelian category; the internal
shift $\{r\}$ is an automorphism of $A_m\text{-mod}$; each $P_i$ is a finite
graded projective left $A_m$-module and each ${}_iP$ a finite graded projective
right $A_m$-module, generated by $e_i$.

**Notation.** The source writes $P_i=A_m(i)$ for the summand $A_me_i$, and
$\{r\}$ for the internal shift; the parentheses in $A_m(i)$ are part of that
summand notation and never denote a shift. On this page only the braces $\{r\}$
denote the internal shift, and only the brackets $[r]$ of
[[def-bounded-projective-homotopy-category-for-a-m]] denote the homological
shift, which is not defined yet.

Fix $m\ge1$, let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]] with vertex idempotents
$e_j=(j)$ and internal degree, and let $A_m\text{-mod}$ be the category of
[[def-graded-khovanov-seidel-module-category-and-projectives]].

**The vertex modules.** For $0\le i\le m$ let $S_i$ be the graded left
$A_m$-module whose underlying graded abelian group is
$$(S_i)_0=\mathbb Z,\qquad (S_i)_d=0\quad(d\ne0),$$
and on which a path $p$ of $\mathbb Z\Gamma_m$ acts by
$$e_i\cdot1=1,\qquad e_j\cdot1=0\ (j\ne i),\qquad p\cdot1=0\text{ for every positive-length path }p.$$
Equivalently, $e_i$ acts as the identity, every other vertex idempotent acts as
zero, and every path of positive length acts as zero. The claims that this
assignment is well defined on the quotient $A_m$, that it makes $S_i$ a
finitely generated graded left $A_m$-module and that it is not the zero module
are proved below, so the notation denotes.

**Prime quotients.** For a prime $p$, $pS_i$ is the $A_m$-submodule generated
by $p\cdot1$ and $S_i/pS_i$ is the quotient module; it is the corresponding
$\mathbb Z/p$ **vertex module**, that is the graded left $A_m$-module
$(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)$ in internal degree $0$, with the induced action in
which $e_i$ acts as the identity and every other vertex idempotent and every
positive-length path acts as zero. The sequence
$$0\to S_i\xrightarrow{p}S_i\to S_i/pS_i\to0$$
is degreewise exact for every prime $p$; exactness at both non-end terms is
proved below, so the notation denotes.

**Shifts.** The internal shifts of $S_i$ are inherited from $A_m\text{-mod}$:
$S_i\{r\}$ is the internal shift of the definition of
[[def-graded-khovanov-seidel-module-category-and-projectives]], so that
$(S_i\{r\})_{r}=\mathbb Z$ and all other graded pieces vanish and the same
action rule applies. The vertex module $S_i$ is the quotient of the vertex
projective $P_i=A_me_i$ by its positive-length-path submodule; the
identifications with the quotients $P_i/A_m\{u_{i-1},d_i,r_i\}$ (omitting $u_{-1}$, $d_m$ and $r_0$ at the endpoints, and writing $r_i=(i|i-1|i)$ for $1\le i\le m$) and with the
$\mathbb Z/p$ reductions are proved on the pages that use them.

Fix $m\ge1$ and $0\le i\le m$, let $A_m$ be the type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]], let $A_m\text{-mod}$ be the
category of [[def-graded-khovanov-seidel-module-category-and-projectives]] with
vertex projectives $P_j=A_me_j$ and internal shifts $\{p\}$, and let $S_i$ and
$S_i/pS_i$ be the vertex modules of [[def-vertex-khovanov-seidel-modules]].

Write $j(p,q):=i+p-q$ and put
$$C_{p,q}:=\begin{cases}P_{j(p,q)}\{p\},& p\ge0,\ q\ge0,\ p\le m-i,\ q\le i+p,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$
so that the nonzero entries form the staircase
$$0\le p\le m-i,\qquad 0\le q\le i+p,$$
on which the projective index $j=i+p-q$ runs from $j=i+p$ down to $j=0$. Let
$$h_{p,q}:C_{p,q}\to C_{p-1,q},\quad x\mapsto x\cdot(j(p,q)\,\big|\,j(p,q)-1),$$
$$v_{p,q}:C_{p,q}\to C_{p,q-1},\quad x\mapsto(-1)^p\,x\cdot(j(p,q)\,\big|\,j(p,q)+1),$$
where a symbol $(j|j-1)$ with $j=0$, a symbol $(j|j+1)$ with $j=m$, and any
symbol whose source or target module is zero denote the zero map, and where right multiplication
by a path $\alpha$ means $x\mapsto x\alpha$ in the ring $A_m$. Then:

1. $(C,h,v)$ is a first-quadrant homological double complex of graded
   $A_m$-modules, and its direct-sum total complex
   $\operatorname{Tot}_\bullet$, with differential $d=h+v$ and
   $\operatorname{Tot}_n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}C_{p,q}$, is a finite graded
   projective resolution of $S_i$: every term is a finite direct sum of internal
   shifts of the $P_j$, only finitely many terms are nonzero, $H_0$ is
   $C_{0,0}=P_i$ modulo the image of $d_1$ and $H_n(\operatorname{Tot})=0$
   for $n\ne0$, the augmentation being the quotient map
   $P_i\to P_i/A_m\{u_{i-1},d_i,r_i\}\cong S_i$, with the endpoint omissions of [[def-vertex-khovanov-seidel-modules]].
2. For every prime $p$, the mapping cone of multiplication by $p$ on
   $\operatorname{Tot}_\bullet$ is a finite graded projective resolution of
   $S_i/pS_i$.

Let $A$ be an object of an abelian category. A **projective resolution of $A$** is an augmented chain complex $$\cdots \to P_2\to P_1\to P_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A\to0$$ such that every $P_n$ is projective and the augmented complex is exact at every displayed term.

Thus a projective resolution is an exact way of recovering $A$ from projective objects arranged in homological degrees.

Fix $m\ge1$ and let $A_m\text{-mod}$ be the abelian category of finite
generated graded left $A_m$-modules and degree-zero maps of
[[def-graded-khovanov-seidel-module-category-and-projectives]]. Let
$$0\to M'\xrightarrow{i}M\xrightarrow{q}M''\to0$$
be degreewise exact in $A_m\text{-mod}$, so that $i$ is injective, $q$ is
surjective and $\operatorname{im}i=\ker q$ degreewise, and suppose that $M'$
admits a finite graded projective resolution of length at most $a$ and $M''$
one of length at most $b$, in the sense that the resolutions
$$0\to P'_a\to\cdots\to P'_1\to P'_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon'}M'\to0,\qquad 0\to P''_b\to\cdots\to P''_1\to P''_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon''}M''\to0$$
consist of finitely generated graded projective modules with $P'_n=0$ for
$n>a$ and $P''_n=0$ for $n>b$. Then $M$ admits a finite graded projective
resolution of length at most $\max(a,b)$, that is, there is an exact sequence
$$0\to P_{\max(a,b)}\to\cdots\to P_1\to P_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}M\to0$$
of finitely generated graded projectives with $P_n=0$ for
$n>\max(a,b)$.

In particular, writing $\operatorname{pd}$ for the least such length (so that
$\operatorname{pd}X=0$ exactly when $X$ is finite graded projective, and the
zero module has $\operatorname{pd}0=0$), every degreewise extension of two
objects of finite projective dimension has finite projective dimension with
$\operatorname{pd}M\le\max(\operatorname{pd}M',\operatorname{pd}M'')$. The
argument is a horseshoe construction carried out on elements of graded modules
and selects only finitely many lifts; it uses no choice principle and no
arbitrary-abelian-category element chase.

Every finitely generated abelian group $G$ has unique canonical decompositions

$$G\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus\mathbb Z/(n_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb Z/(n_t),\qquad 1<n_1\mid\cdots\mid n_t,$$

and

$$G\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus\bigoplus_{p,j}\mathbb Z/(p^{e_{p,j}}),$$

where $r$ and the finite torsion data are unique up to the stated order. The torsion summand is finite. The trivial group has $r=0$ and empty torsion data.

Let $A$ be a graded $k$-algebra and let $P$ be a graded left $A$-module. Then $P$
is finite graded projective
([[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]]) if and only if $P$ is a
degree-zero direct summand of a finite direct sum of internal shifts
$A\{r_1\}\oplus\cdots\oplus A\{r_n\}$. In particular every finite direct sum of
shifts $A\{r_j\}$ is a projective object of $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$, and this
conclusion uses no assumption of arbitrary-index choice.

derivations.claim: *The positive-length ideal $J$ and its powers.* Let $J\le A_m$ be the $\mathbb Z$-span of the classes of the paths of positive length. By [L2] every positive-length basis element is one of the arrows $u_i$, $d_i$ for $0\le i<m$ or the returns $(i|i-1|i)$ for $1\le i\le m$, while the monotone and reverse monotone length-two paths have class $0$ in $I_m$ by [F1]; hence $J=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}(\mathbb Zu_i+\mathbb Zd_i)+\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbb Z(i|i-1|i)$ and $A_m=\bigl(\bigoplus_{i=0}^m\mathbb Ze_i\bigr)\oplus J$ as graded abelian groups, and $J$ is a two-sided ideal because multiplying a positive-length class on either side either concatenates to a longer path or gives $0$ by [F3]. Multiplying two positive-length basis classes gives either a noncomposable product, hence $0$ by [F3], a path of length at least three, hence $0$ by [L2], or one of the products $u_id_i=(i|i+1|i)$ and $d_iu_i=(i+1|i|i+1)$ for $0\le i<m$, the product $u_0d_0=(0|1|0)$ having class $0$ by [L2]; at each interior vertex the two returns agree by [F1], so $J^2$ is the $\mathbb Z$-span of the returns $(1|0|1),\dots,(m|m-1|m)$, and every product of three positive-length classes is a path of length at least three or $0$ and hence vanishes by [L2], so $J^3=0$.

*The graded quotient ring $E=A_m/J$.* By step 1.1 the composite $\bigoplus_{i=0}^m\mathbb Ze_i\to A_m\to A_m/J$ is a $\mathbb Z$-module isomorphism, and by [F3] the vertex classes satisfy $e_ie_j=\delta_{ij}e_i$ and $1=\sum_ie_i$, so $E=A_m/J$ is isomorphic as a unital ring to the product $\prod_{i=0}^m\mathbb Z$ with coordinate idempotents the images of the $e_i$; these images have degree $0$ by [F1], so $E$ is concentrated in internal degree $0$. In particular $E$ is a free abelian group of rank $m+1$, and each component $e_iE$ is $\mathbb Ze_i$.

*The three-step filtration of $M$ and its finitely generated quotients.* Let $M$ be a finitely generated graded left $A_m$-module with homogeneous generators $x_1,\dots,x_N$. The sets $JM\supseteq J^2M\supseteq J^3M=0$ are graded $A_m$-submodules, and the quotients $Q_1:=M/JM$, $Q_2:=JM/J^2M$, $Q_3:=J^2M$ are annihilated by $J$ since $JQ_1=0$, $JQ_2=J^2M/J^3M=0$ and $JQ_3=J^3M=0$ by step 1.1, so each $Q_k$ is a graded $E$-module by step 2.1. Each $Q_k$ is finitely generated as an $E$-module: $JM$ is the $A_m$-submodule generated by the finitely many products $gx_j$ with $g$ in the finite basis set $\{u_i,d_i:0\le i<m\}\cup\{(i|i-1|i):1\le i\le m\}$, and $J^2M$ by the finitely many $ghx_j$ with $g,h$ in that set, so both are finitely generated, and $Q_1$ is a quotient of $M$.

*Finitely generated graded $E$-modules decompose into abelian groups.* Let $N$ be a finitely generated graded left $E$-module with homogeneous generators $y_1,\dots,y_s$ of degrees $d_1,\dots,d_s$. Since $E$ is concentrated in degree $0$ by step 2.1, $N_d=\sum_{j:d_j=d}\mathbb Ey_j$, so $N_d=0$ for $d\notin\{d_1,\dots,d_s\}$; writing $N_{d,i}:=e_iN_d$ gives $N_d=\bigoplus_{i=0}^mN_{d,i}$ by the idempotent decomposition of step 2.1, and each $N_{d,i}$ is the image of $\mathbb Z^{s_d}$ under the map that reads the $i$-th coordinate, where $s_d$ is the number of generators of degree $d$, so $N_{d,i}$ is a finitely generated abelian group. Hence $N$ is the finite direct sum of the graded $E$-modules obtained by placing $N_{d,i}$ in degree $d$, on which $e_i$ acts as the identity of $N_{d,i}$ and $e_j$ with $j\ne i$ acts as $0$.

*Filtrations of the pieces with vertex-module quotients.* By [F9] the finitely generated abelian group $N_{d,i}$ of step 3.2 is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^r\oplus\bigoplus_j\mathbb Z/(p_j^{e_j})$, so it carries a finite $\mathbb Z$-submodule filtration with successive quotients isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$ or to $\mathbb Z/p$: add the $r$ free cyclic summands one at a time, and for each cyclic summand $C=\mathbb Z/p^{e}$ use the chain $0\subseteq p^{e-1}C\subseteq\cdots\subseteq pC\subseteq C$, whose successive quotients $p^jC/p^{j+1}C$ are cyclic of order $p$. Each of these submodules is stable under the $E$-action of step 3.2, because $e_i$ acts as the identity and every $e_j$ with $j\ne i$ as $0$ on the piece placed in degree $d$, so the filtration is a filtration by $E$-submodules and, by [L5], its successive quotients are the internal shifts $S_i\{d\}$ in the free case and $S_i/pS_i\{d\}$ in the cyclic torsion case. Splicing the finitely many such filtrations over the finite index set of step 3.2 into the three-step filtration $0\subseteq J^2M\subseteq JM\subseteq M$ of step 3.1 by taking preimages of filter pieces under the displayed quotient maps yields a finite filtration $0=F_0\subseteq F_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_t=M$ of $M$ by graded $A_m$-submodules whose successive quotients $F_k/F_{k-1}$ are internal shifts of $S_i$ or of $S_i/pS_i$ for some $0\le i\le m$ and some prime $p$.

*The uniform bound on the pieces.* Let $0\le i\le m$. By [L6] the resolution of $S_i$ is the total complex of the staircase double complex with nonzero entries $C_{p,q}=P_{i+p-q}\{p\}$ on $0\le p\le m-i$, $0\le q\le i+p$, so its nonzero terms lie in total degrees $n=p+q$ with $0\le n\le(m-i)+m=2m-i$; hence $S_i$ has a finite graded projective resolution of length at most $2m-i\le2m$, and the mapping cone of [L6] adds exactly one homological degree, so $S_i/pS_i$ has a finite graded projective resolution of length at most $2m-i+1\le2m+1$. Since the internal shift is an automorphism of $A_m\text{-mod}$ by [L4] that carries finite graded projectives to finite graded projectives — a finite graded projective is a degree-zero direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts $A_m\{r_j\}$ by [L10], and shifting that decomposition by $d$ presents $P\{d\}$ as a degree-zero direct summand of the finite direct sum of the shifts $A_m\{r_j+d\}$ — every internal shift of $S_i$ or of $S_i/pS_i$ admits a finite graded projective resolution of length at most $2m+1$.

*Extension-stability over the finite filtration.* Let $L:=2m+1$. We show by induction on $k$ that every member $F_k$ of the filtration of step 4.1 has a finite graded projective resolution of length at most $L$. For $k=0$ the zero module has the zero resolution $0\to F_0\to0$ of length $0\le L$. For $k\ge1$ the sequence $0\to F_{k-1}\to F_k\to F_k/F_{k-1}\to0$ is degreewise exact in $A_m\text{-mod}$; step 5.1 gives the quotient $F_k/F_{k-1}$ a finite graded projective resolution of length at most $L$, the inductive hypothesis gives one for $F_{k-1}$, and [L8] then gives one for $F_k$ of length at most $\max(L,L)=L$, using only the finitely many lifts of that construction.

*Conclusion.* Every finitely generated graded left $A_m$-module $M$ has a finite graded projective resolution of length at most $L=2m+1$, namely the one built in step 6.1 for $k=t$; by [L7] this is a projective resolution in the sense of the statement, its length bound depends only on $m$, and the successive quotients of the filtration producing it are internal shifts of the vertex modules $S_i$ and their prime quotients, so $\operatorname{pd}M\le2m+1$ uniformly on $A_m\text{-mod}$ and the finite graded module category has finite homological dimension. The proof used only the finite path basis, the structure theory of a finitely generated abelian group, the finitely many lifts of [L8] and the explicit resolutions of [L6], and it selected no family indexed by an infinite set, so no choice principle is assumed.

[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]], graded by internal degree, with

$d_i:=(i+1|i)$.

**The finite module category.** $A_m\text{-mod}$ is the category whose objects
are the **finitely generated graded left $A_m$-modules** and whose morphisms are
the **degree-zero $A_m$-linear maps** $f:M\to N$, that is
$f(M_d)\subseteq N_d$ for every $d$, with composition of maps. Throughout this
page every left module, right module and bimodule over $A_m$ is graded and every
homomorphism is degree-zero unless stated otherwise. Finite generation is in the
sense of [[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]], and graded
modules, degree-zero maps and internal shifts are those of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]].

**Internal shift.** For $r\in\mathbb Z$ and a graded left $A_m$-module $M$ the
**internal shift** $M\{r\}$ is the graded module with
$$(M\{r\})_d=M_{d-r}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
carrying the same left $A_m$-action as $M$. The shift $\{1\}$ moves the grading
upwards by one: an element of $M_d$ is an element of $(M\{1\})_{d+1}$.

**Vertex projectives.** Put
$$P_i:=A_me_i,\qquad {}_iP:=e_iA_m\qquad(0\le i\le m),$$
equipped with the grading in which a homogeneous element of $A_m$ of degree $d$
lies in degree $d$. Because paths are written left to right and the product is
concatenation, $P_i$ consists of the classes of the paths **ending** at $i$ and
${}_iP$ of the classes of the paths **beginning** at $i$. The algebra splits as
$$A_m=\bigoplus_{i=0}^mP_i=\bigoplus_{i=0}^m{}_iP$$
as a left, respectively right, module over itself; the decomposition into vertex
projectives is displayed as proved below.

**Claims proved below.** $A_m\text{-mod}$ is an abelian category; the internal
shift $\{r\}$ is an automorphism of $A_m\text{-mod}$; each $P_i$ is a finite
graded projective left $A_m$-module and each ${}_iP$ a finite graded projective
right $A_m$-module, generated by $e_i$.

$\{r\}$ for the internal shift; the parentheses in $A_m(i)$ are part of that

Let $m\ge1$ and let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]]. As a graded abelian group $A_m$
is free of rank $4m+1$, with basis the images of the $4m+1$ paths
$$(0),\dots,(m);\qquad (0|1),\dots,(m-1|m);\qquad (1|0),\dots,(m|m-1);\qquad (1|0|1),\dots,(m|m-1|m),$$
that is: the $m+1$ vertices, the $2m$ arrows, and one degree-one length-two
**return** at each vertex $i=1,\dots,m$. Every path of length at least three has
class $0$ in $A_m$, the monotone length-two path $(i-1|i|i+1)$ and its reverse
$(i+1|i|i-1)$ have class $0$ for $0<i<m$, the return $(0|1|0)$ has class $0$,
and at an interior vertex $0<i<m$ the two returns $(i|i+1|i)$ and $(i|i-1|i)$
have the same class. In particular $A_m$ is a finitely generated free abelian
group, so its underlying $\mathbb Z$-module is free of finite rank $4m+1$.

A **finite quiver** is a quadruple $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$ in which $Q_0$ and $Q_1$
are finite sets, whose elements are called **vertices** and **arrows**, together
with maps $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$ assigning to an arrow $a$ its **source** $s(a)$ and
its **target** $t(a)$; one draws $a:s(a)\to t(a)$. Both sets are finite and no
further structure is assumed: $Q$ may have several arrows with the same source
and target, and an arrow may be a loop, although the quivers used below have
neither property.

A **directed path** in $Q$ of length $l\ge0$ consists of vertices
$v_0,\ldots,v_l$ and specified arrows $a_j:v_{j-1}\to v_j$ for $1\le j\le l$.
Write it as $p=(v_0\xrightarrow{a_1}v_1\xrightarrow{a_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{a_l}v_l)$.
The arrows are part of the data: distinct parallel arrows give distinct paths.
A path of length zero is a single vertex $(v)$, called a **vertex idempotent**.
Write $|p|:=l$, $s(p):=v_0$ and $t(p):=v_l$ for its **length**, **source** and
**target**. When the arrows are determined by their endpoints, as in the doubled
lines used below, abbreviate this by $(v_0|\cdots|v_l)$; in formulas for a
general quiver this abbreviation retains the specified arrows as implicit data.
Paths $p$ and $q$ are **composable** if $t(p)=s(q)$. Their **concatenation**
$pq$ traverses the arrow sequence of $p$ first and then that of $q$, retaining
all arrow labels; in the abbreviated notation it is
$$(v_0|\cdots|v_l)(v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'})=(v_0|\cdots|v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'}).$$

The **integral path ring** $\mathbb ZQ$ is the free abelian group on the set of
all directed paths of $Q$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]),
with multiplication defined on basis paths by
$$(v_0|\cdots|v_l)(w_0|\cdots|w_{l'}):= \begin{cases}(v_0|\cdots|v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'}),&v_l=w_0,\\ 0,&v_l\ne w_0,\end{cases}$$
and extended by $\mathbb Z$-bilinearity. Its unit is the finite sum
$$1_{\mathbb ZQ}=\sum_{v\in Q_0}(v)$$
of the vertex idempotents, which is a finite sum because $Q_0$ is finite.

**Endpoint conventions.** For a path $p$ and vertices $u,v$ one has
$$(u)\,p=\begin{cases}p,&s(p)=u,\\ 0,&s(p)\ne u,\end{cases} \qquad p\,(v)=\begin{cases}p,&t(p)=v,\\ 0,&t(p)\ne v.\end{cases}$$
Consequently the vertex idempotents are mutually orthogonal,
$(u)(v)=\delta_{uv}(v)$, and they decompose the ring as
$$\mathbb ZQ=\bigoplus_{u,v\in Q_0}(u)\,\mathbb ZQ\,(v),$$
the sum of the free abelian groups spanned by the paths with source $u$ and
target $v$. In the quotient rings used below, the analogous statements read:
the right ideal generated by the image of $(u)$ is spanned by the classes of paths with source

*$U_i$ is a graded $(A_m,A_m)$-bimodule.* The left action $a\cdot(x\otimes y)=(ax)\otimes y$ is well defined because $P_i$ is a left $A_m$-module and additive in each variable, and it is homogeneous because $A_m$ is graded with $(A_m)_l(P_i)_d\subseteq(P_i)_{l+d}$ for all internal degrees $l,d$, with the vertex index $i$ fixed; the right action $(x\otimes y)\cdot a=x\otimes(ya)$ is well defined because ${}_iP$ is a right $A_m$-module, and homogeneous for the same reason on the second factor. The two actions commute because the first acts on the first tensor factor and the second on the second, and both are unital; so $U_i$ is a graded $(A_m,A_m)$-bimodule by [L3] and the bimodule convention of [L3].

*$U_i$ is finite graded projective on the left.* Let $y_1,\dots,y_R$ be the homogeneous basis of ${}_iP$ of step 1.1 with degrees $d_1,\dots,d_R$; an element of $U_i$ is a finite sum $\sum_jx_j\otimes y_j$ with $x_j\in P_i$, and the assignment $(x_1,\dots,x_R)\mapsto\sum_jx_j\otimes y_j$ defines an $A_m$-linear bijection $\bigoplus_{j=1}^RP_i\{d_j\}\to U_i$ that is degree-zero for the total grading of [L3], since $P_i\{d_j\}$ has $(P_i\{d_j\})_{e}= (P_i)_{e-d_j}$ and $x\otimes y_j$ has degree $\deg x+d_j$. The module $P_i$ is finite graded projective by [L1], its internal shift is finite graded projective by [L5], and a finite direct sum of finite graded projectives is finite graded projective by [L5] again, applied to the direct-summand characterization; hence $U_i\cong\bigoplus_jP_i\{d_j\}$ is a finite graded projective left $A_m$-module, in particular finitely generated by [L6].

*$U_i$ is finite graded projective on the right.* The mirrored argument with a homogeneous basis $x_1,\dots,x_S$ of $P_i$ and the assignment $(y_1,\dots,y_S)\mapsto\sum_kx_k\otimes y_k$ identifies $U_i$ with $\bigoplus_k{}_iP\{d'_k\}$ as a graded right $A_m$-module, where $d'_k$ is the degree of $x_k$; each ${}_iP$ is finite graded projective on the right by [L1], its shifts are again finite graded projective by the opposite-ring instance of [L5], and finite direct sums are finite graded projective, so $U_i$ is a finite graded projective right $A_m$-module.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]]. As a graded abelian group $A_m$
is free of rank $4m+1$, with basis the images of the $4m+1$ paths
$$(0),\dots,(m);\qquad (0|1),\dots,(m-1|m);\qquad (1|0),\dots,(m|m-1);\qquad (1|0|1),\dots,(m|m-1|m),$$
that is: the $m+1$ vertices, the $2m$ arrows, and one degree-one length-two
**return** at each vertex $i=1,\dots,m$. Every path of length at least three has
class $0$ in $A_m$, the monotone length-two path $(i-1|i|i+1)$ and its reverse
$(i+1|i|i-1)$ have class $0$ for $0<i<m$, the return $(0|1|0)$ has class $0$,
and at an interior vertex $0<i<m$ the two returns $(i|i+1|i)$ and $(i|i-1|i)$
have the same class. In particular $A_m$ is a finitely generated free abelian
group, so its underlying $\mathbb Z$-module is free of finite rank $4m+1$.

**The algebra.** For $m\ge1$, let $I_m\trianglelefteq\mathbb Z\Gamma_m$ be the
two-sided ideal generated by the elements
$$(i-1|i|i+1),\qquad (i+1|i|i-1),\qquad (i|i+1|i)-(i|i-1|i),\qquad (0|1|0),$$

family is empty and only $(0|1|0)$ is imposed. The **Khovanov–Seidel type A
algebra** is the quotient ring
$$A_m:=\mathbb Z\Gamma_m\big/I_m$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]), whose elements are written as cosets of paths.

**The finite module category.** $A_m\text{-mod}$ is the category whose objects
are the **finitely generated graded left $A_m$-modules** and whose morphisms are
the **degree-zero $A_m$-linear maps** $f:M\to N$, that is
$f(M_d)\subseteq N_d$ for every $d$, with composition of maps. Throughout this
page every left module, right module and bimodule over $A_m$ is graded and every
homomorphism is degree-zero unless stated otherwise. Finite generation is in the
sense of [[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]], and graded
modules, degree-zero maps and internal shifts are those of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]].

$$M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N\cong\bigoplus_{i,j\in\mathbb Z}M_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N_j.$$

$G_d:=\bigoplus_{i+j=d}M_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N_j$.

([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]), where

homogeneous relation belongs to $G_{i+\ell+j}$, since the two module actions

$$M\otimes_AN=\bigoplus_{d\in\mathbb Z}(M\otimes_AN)_d,\qquad (M\otimes_AN)_d:=(G_d+\mathcal R_A)/\mathcal R_A,$$

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,Q):=\bigl\{f\in\operatorname{Hom}_A^{\mathrm{ungr}}(P,Q)\mid f(P_i)\subseteq Q_{i+d}\ \text{for all }i\in\mathbb Z\bigr\},\qquad \operatorname{HOM}_A(P,Q):=\bigoplus_{d\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,Q).$$

$\operatorname{Hom}_A^{\mathrm{ungr}}(P,Q)$, and the sum is direct: if

citations.quote:
A **finite quiver** is a quadruple $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$ in which $Q_0$ and $Q_1$
are finite sets, whose elements are called **vertices** and **arrows**, together
with maps $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$ assigning to an arrow $a$ its **source** $s(a)$ and
its **target** $t(a)$; one draws $a:s(a)\to t(a)$. Both sets are finite and no
further structure is assumed: $Q$ may have several arrows with the same source
and target, and an arrow may be a loop, although the quivers used below have
neither property.

A **directed path** in $Q$ of length $l\ge0$ consists of vertices
$v_0,\ldots,v_l$ and specified arrows $a_j:v_{j-1}\to v_j$ for $1\le j\le l$.
Write it as $p=(v_0\xrightarrow{a_1}v_1\xrightarrow{a_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{a_l}v_l)$.
The arrows are part of the data: distinct parallel arrows give distinct paths.
A path of length zero is a single vertex $(v)$, called a **vertex idempotent**.
Write $|p|:=l$, $s(p):=v_0$ and $t(p):=v_l$ for its **length**, **source** and
**target**. When the arrows are determined by their endpoints, as in the doubled
lines used below, abbreviate this by $(v_0|\cdots|v_l)$; in formulas for a
general quiver this abbreviation retains the specified arrows as implicit data.
Paths $p$ and $q$ are **composable** if $t(p)=s(q)$. Their **concatenation**
$pq$ traverses the arrow sequence of $p$ first and then that of $q$, retaining
all arrow labels; in the abbreviated notation it is
$$(v_0|\cdots|v_l)(v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'})=(v_0|\cdots|v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'}).$$

The **integral path ring** $\mathbb ZQ$ is the free abelian group on the set of
all directed paths of $Q$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]),
with multiplication defined on basis paths by
$$(v_0|\cdots|v_l)(w_0|\cdots|w_{l'}):= \begin{cases}(v_0|\cdots|v_l|w_1|\cdots|w_{l'}),&v_l=w_0,\\ 0,&v_l\ne w_0,\end{cases}$$
and extended by $\mathbb Z$-bilinearity. Its unit is the finite sum
$$1_{\mathbb ZQ}=\sum_{v\in Q_0}(v)$$
of the vertex idempotents, which is a finite sum because $Q_0$ is finite.

**Endpoint conventions.** For a path $p$ and vertices $u,v$ one has
$$(u)\,p=\begin{cases}p,&s(p)=u,\\ 0,&s(p)\ne u,\end{cases} \qquad p\,(v)=\begin{cases}p,&t(p)=v,\\ 0,&t(p)\ne v.\end{cases}$$
Consequently the vertex idempotents are mutually orthogonal,
$(u)(v)=\delta_{uv}(v)$, and they decompose the ring as
$$\mathbb ZQ=\bigoplus_{u,v\in Q_0}(u)\,\mathbb ZQ\,(v),$$
the sum of the free abelian groups spanned by the paths with source $u$ and
target $v$. In the quotient rings used below, the analogous statements read:
the right ideal generated by the image of $(u)$ is spanned by the classes of paths with source
$u$, and the left ideal generated by the image of $(v)$ is spanned by the classes of paths with target
$v$, so that $A\,e_i$ consists of the paths **ending** at $i$ and $e_iA$ of the
paths **beginning** at $i$ whenever $A$ is a quotient of $\mathbb ZQ$ and
$e_i$ is the image of $(i)$.

**Empty quiver.** For $Q_0=Q_1=\varnothing$ the set of paths is empty, so
$\mathbb ZQ$ is the zero abelian group, the displayed sum for $1$ is empty and
$1=0$; this is the zero ring, and every statement below is trivial there. All
quivers occurring on this page are the doubled lines $\Gamma_m$ with $m\ge1$,
which have $m+1\ge2$ vertices.

**Vertex projectives.** Put
$$P_i:=A_me_i,\qquad {}_iP:=e_iA_m\qquad(0\le i\le m),$$
equipped with the grading in which a homogeneous element of $A_m$ of degree $d$
lies in degree $d$. Because paths are written left to right and the product is
concatenation, $P_i$ consists of the classes of the paths **ending** at $i$ and
${}_iP$ of the classes of the paths **beginning** at $i$. The algebra splits as
$$A_m=\bigoplus_{i=0}^mP_i=\bigoplus_{i=0}^m{}_iP$$
as a left, respectively right, module over itself; the decomposition into vertex
projectives is displayed as proved below.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]]. As a graded abelian group $A_m$
is free of rank $4m+1$, with basis the images of the $4m+1$ paths
$$(0),\dots,(m);\qquad (0|1),\dots,(m-1|m);\qquad (1|0),\dots,(m|m-1);\qquad (1|0|1),\dots,(m|m-1|m),$$
that is: the $m+1$ vertices, the $2m$ arrows, and one degree-one length-two
**return** at each vertex $i=1,\dots,m$. Every path of length at least three has
class $0$ in $A_m$, the monotone length-two path $(i-1|i|i+1)$ and its reverse
$(i+1|i|i-1)$ have class $0$ for $0<i<m$, the return $(0|1|0)$ has class $0$,
and at an interior vertex $0<i<m$ the two returns $(i|i+1|i)$ and $(i|i-1|i)$
have the same class. In particular $A_m$ is a finitely generated free abelian
group, so its underlying $\mathbb Z$-module is free of finite rank $4m+1$.

**Internal degree.** The **internal degree** of a path is the integer
$$\deg(v_0|v_1|\cdots|v_l):=\#\{\,j:0\le j<l,\ v_{j+1}=v_j-1\,\},$$
the number of steps in which the path moves **down**; so a vertex and an
ascending arrow $(i|i+1)$ have degree $0$, while a descending arrow
$(i+1|i)$ has degree $1$. This number is additive under concatenation,
$\deg(pq)=\deg(p)+\deg(q)$.

**Total internal degree on the balanced tensor product.** Let $A$ be a graded
$k$-algebra, $M$ a graded right $A$-module and $N$ a graded left $A$-module
([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). First use the canonical
decomposition of the ordinary tensor product of the underlying abelian groups
$$M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N\cong\bigoplus_{i,j\in\mathbb Z}M_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N_j.$$
Its inverse sends $m\otimes n$ to the finite sum
$\sum_{i,j}m_i\otimes n_j$, where $m=\sum_i m_i$ and $n=\sum_jn_j$ are their
homogeneous decompositions; the two maps are inverse because they agree with
the identity on homogeneous elementary tensors. Give the summand
$M_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N_j$ total degree $i+j$, and write
$G_d:=\bigoplus_{i+j=d}M_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N_j$.

The balanced tensor product
$M\otimes_AN=(M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N)/\mathcal R_A$
([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]), where
$\mathcal R_A$ is generated by the balance relations
$(ma)\otimes n-m\otimes(an)$. These relations are generated by the homogeneous
ones: for $m=\sum_i m_i$, $a=\sum_\ell a_\ell$ and $n=\sum_jn_j$, the relation
is the finite sum of
$(m_i a_\ell)\otimes n_j-m_i\otimes(a_\ell n_j)$ over $i,\ell,j$. Each such
homogeneous relation belongs to $G_{i+\ell+j}$, since the two module actions
preserve total degree. Thus $\mathcal R_A=\bigoplus_d(\mathcal R_A\cap G_d)$,
and

$$M\otimes_AN=\bigoplus_{d\in\mathbb Z}(M\otimes_AN)_d,\qquad (M\otimes_AN)_d:=(G_d+\mathcal R_A)/\mathcal R_A,$$

is a graded abelian group. For homogeneous $m\in M_i$ and $n\in N_j$ the
elementary tensor $m\otimes n$ has **total internal degree** $i+j$; every tensor
is a finite sum of homogeneous elementary tensors, and the balancing relations
used in the quotient are homogeneous. This grading is the only grading used
below, and it introduces no sign.

**Outer actions.** If $M$ is a graded $(B,A)$-bimodule and $N$ a graded left
$A$-module, then the action $b(m\otimes n):=(bm)\otimes n$ of
[[thm-bimodule-actions-induced-on-tensor-products]] makes $M\otimes_AN$ a graded
left $B$-module: the action is homogeneous because homogeneous $b\in B_l$ sends
$m\otimes n$ of degree $i+j$ to an element of degree $l+i+j$. Symmetrically, if
$N$ is a graded $(A,C)$-bimodule, the action
$(m\otimes n)c:=m\otimes(nc)$ makes $M\otimes_AN$ a graded right $C$-module, and
the two outer actions commute when both are present.

**Homogeneous Hom.** For graded left $A$-modules $P,Q$, with
$\operatorname{Hom}_A^{\mathrm{ungr}}(P,Q)$ the abelian group of all $A$-linear
maps $P\to Q$, put

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,Q):=\bigl\{f\in\operatorname{Hom}_A^{\mathrm{ungr}}(P,Q)\mid f(P_i)\subseteq Q_{i+d}\ \text{for all }i\in\mathbb Z\bigr\},\qquad \operatorname{HOM}_A(P,Q):=\bigoplus_{d\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,Q).$$

Each $\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,Q)$ is a subgroup of
$\operatorname{Hom}_A^{\mathrm{ungr}}(P,Q)$, and the sum is direct: if
$f=\sum_df_d=\sum_df'_d$ with $f_d,f'_d\in\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}$, then for
$p\in P_i$ the element $f(p)$ has homogeneous components
$f_d(p)\in Q_{i+d}$, and comparison of the graded components in $Q$ gives
$f_d(p)=f'_d(p)$ for every $d$ and $p$, so $f_d=f'_d$. Thus
$\operatorname{HOM}_A(P,Q)$ is a graded abelian group whose degree-$d$ part is
$\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,Q)$, and the degree-zero morphisms are
$\operatorname{Hom}_{A,0}(P,Q)$. By definition $\operatorname{HOM}_A(P,Q)$
consists of the finite sums of homogeneous $A$-linear maps, so
$\operatorname{HOM}_A(P,Q)\subseteq\operatorname{Hom}_A^{\mathrm{ungr}}(P,Q)$
with equality only when every $A$-linear map has bounded spread in degree.

**The associative left action.** If $M$ is a graded $(B,A)$-bimodule and $Y$ a
graded left $B$-module, then $\operatorname{HOM}_B(M,Y)$ carries a left
$A$-module structure

$$(a\cdot f)(m):=f(ma)\qquad(a\in A,\ m\in M),$$

which is homogeneous: for $a\in A_i$ and $f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{B,d}(M,Y)$ one
has $ma\in M_{l+i}$ for $m\in M_l$, hence $(a\cdot f)(m)\in Y_{l+i+d}$ and
$a\cdot f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{B,d+i}(M,Y)$. The action is associative and
unital by the module axioms of $M$, so $\operatorname{HOM}_B(M,Y)$ is a graded
left $A$-module and an object of $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$. The same formula
defines an action on the full ungraded $\operatorname{Hom}$ group, where it is
denoted by the same symbol.

Fix $m\ge1$, let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra with its internal
grading, and let $A_m\text{-mod}$ be the category of
[[def-graded-khovanov-seidel-module-category-and-projectives]] with vertex
projectives
$$P_i=A_me_i\qquad(\text{paths ending at }i),\qquad {}_iP=e_iA_m\qquad(\text{paths beginning at }i).$$
For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$U_i:=P_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}{}_iP,$$
the tensor product over $\mathbb Z$ of the left $A_m$-module $P_i$ and the
right $A_m$-module ${}_iP$, with the left $A_m$-action $a\cdot(x\otimes y):=(ax)\otimes y$
on the first factor and the right $A_m$-action $(x\otimes y)\cdot a:=x\otimes(ya)$
on the second; the two actions commute because they act on different factors.
Its **grading** is the total internal degree of
[[def-graded-balanced-tensor-product-and-homogeneous-hom]]: an elementary
tensor of homogeneous elements of degrees $p$ and $q$ has degree $p+q$, which
agrees with that construction applied to the right module ${}_iP$ and the left
module $P_i$ under the canonical flip of the commutative ground ring
$\mathbb Z$. The claims that $U_i$ is a graded $(A_m,A_m)$-bimodule, that it is
finite graded projective as a left module and as a right module, and that it is
flat as an underlying right $A_m$-module are proved below, so the notation
denotes.

2. For every graded left $R$-module $N$ and graded right $R$-module $M$ the
tensor-unit maps $\lambda_N:R\otimes_RN\to N$, $r\otimes n\mapsto rn$, and
$\rho_M:M\otimes_RR\to M$, $m\otimes r\mapsto mr$, are degree-zero isomorphisms,
compatible with outer actions.
